subChunks.title: Geology — Plate Tectonics, Rocks & Minerals

storyBeats.txt: Theodora traced the outline of South America, then Africa. "Look at these coastlines," she said. "In 1912, Alfred Wegener pointed at this fit and proposed that the continents had once been joined. He called it continental drift. The geological community rejected him almost entirely, calling his mechanism absurd. He was right about the observation and right about the conclusion — but he had no mechanism."

"The mechanism came from the ocean floor. In the 1950s and 1960s, oceanographic surveys mapped mid-ocean ridges and measured magnetic anomalies in seafloor rocks — magnetic stripes symmetric about the ridges, recording reversals of Earth's magnetic field. Seafloor spreading. New ocean floor constantly created at ridges, old floor consumed at trenches. The continents were riding on moving plates, just as Wegener had insisted."

"Plate tectonics is the organising framework of Earth science. Earthquakes, volcanoes, mountain ranges, ore deposits, the distribution of fossils, the shape of coastlines — all follow from plates in motion. And beneath it all is a planet still cooling from its formation, its interior convecting, driving the plates above as if on a very slow conveyor belt that has been running for four billion years."

subChunks.hookHtml: Plate tectonics is the unifying theory of Earth science — the framework that explains the distribution of earthquakes, volcanoes, mountain ranges, and ocean basins. Earth's outer shell (lithosphere) is divided into tectonic plates that move across the underlying asthenosphere, driven by mantle convection and slab pull. At plate boundaries — divergent, convergent, and transform — rocks are created, destroyed, and deformed, cycling material through the crust over geological timescales.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Earth's Internal Structure

Layers by composition: Crust (oceanic — mafic basalt, 5–10 km thick; continental — felsic granite, 30–70 km thick), mantle (silicate rock, peridotite; ≈2900 km thick), outer core (liquid iron-nickel, generates magnetic field by convection), inner core (solid iron-nickel, ≈1220 km radius).

Layers by mechanical properties: Lithosphere (rigid crust + uppermost mantle, ≈100 km thick — the plates), asthenosphere (partially molten, ductile mantle — plates 'float' on this layer), mesosphere (lower mantle, rigid despite high temperature due to pressure), outer/inner core.

Heat sources: Residual heat from accretion + radioactive decay of U, Th, K in the mantle. This heat drives mantle convection — the engine of plate tectonics.

Plate Tectonics — Boundaries and Processes

Divergent boundaries: Plates move apart. Mid-ocean ridges: magma upwells from the mantle, cools → new oceanic crust (basalt). The Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreads ≈2.5 cm/year. Continental rifts: East African Rift — continent splits apart → eventually forms new ocean. Generates shallow earthquakes and effusive (low-viscosity) volcanic eruptions.

Convergent boundaries: Plates collide. Three types: (a) Ocean-ocean: denser plate subducts → deep-sea trench, island arc volcanoes (e.g. Japan, Marianas Trench). (b) Ocean-continent: oceanic plate (denser) subducts under continent → Andes-type mountains + coastal volcanoes (e.g. Cascade Range, Andes). (c) Continent-continent: neither subducts (both buoyant) → mountain ranges without volcanoes (e.g. Himalayas — India crashing into Asia). Convergent boundaries generate the deepest earthquakes (Wadati-Benioff zone, down to 700 km depth) and explosive (high-viscosity silica-rich) volcanic eruptions.

Transform boundaries: Plates slide horizontally past each other. No creation or destruction of crust. Generate shallow, powerful earthquakes. Example: San Andreas Fault (California), North Anatolian Fault (Turkey).

Driving forces: Slab pull (cold, dense subducted oceanic lithosphere pulls the rest of the plate behind it) — now thought to be the dominant driver. Ridge push (elevated ridge pushes outward). Mantle convection (asthenosphere flow) — contributes but less than slab pull.

The Rock Cycle

Rocks continuously transform between three types:

  • Igneous rocks: Formed by cooling of magma. Intrusive (plutonic): slow cooling underground → large crystals → granite, gabbro. Extrusive (volcanic): rapid cooling at surface → small crystals or glassy → basalt, rhyolite, obsidian.
  • Sedimentary rocks: Formed from weathered rock fragments (clastic: sandstone, shale), chemical precipitation (limestone, rock salt), or organic material (coal). Deposited in layers (strata) — contain fossils; used for relative dating. Cover ≈75% of Earth's land surface by area (but only ≈5% by volume).
  • Metamorphic rocks: Pre-existing rocks transformed by heat, pressure, or both (without melting). Regional metamorphism at convergent boundaries → slate → phyllite → schist → gneiss (increasing grade). Contact metamorphism around intrusions → hornfels, marble (from limestone), quartzite (from sandstone).

Minerals

A mineral is a naturally occurring, inorganic, crystalline solid with a definite chemical composition. ≈5,000 known minerals. Rock-forming minerals: silicates dominate (quartz, feldspar, mica, pyroxene, amphibole, olivine) — based on SiO₄ tetrahedra. Carbonates (calcite, dolomite), oxides (magnetite, hematite), sulfides (pyrite, galena), halides (halite).

Mineral identification: Hardness (Mohs scale 1–10: talc=1, quartz=7, diamond=10), cleavage (breaking along planes), fracture, lustre (metallic, vitreous, resinous), colour, streak, crystal form, specific gravity.

Earthquakes and Seismology

Earthquakes result from sudden release of accumulated elastic strain along faults. Focus (hypocenter) — point of rupture; epicentre — point on surface directly above. Seismic waves: P-waves (primary, compressional — travel through all materials), S-waves (secondary, shear — only through solids), surface waves (most destructive — Love and Rayleigh waves). The S-wave shadow zone (P-waves refract through liquid outer core; S-waves cannot pass) demonstrates Earth has a liquid outer core.

Magnitude scales: Richter scale (logarithmic — each unit = 10× greater ground motion, ≈31.6× energy). Moment magnitude (Mw) — now preferred, better for very large earthquakes. Mercalli scale — measures intensity (observed effects), not magnitude.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old how scientists figured out that Earth has a liquid outer core and a solid inner core — what observations were the clues, and what physics explains why the outer core is liquid?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: A geologist examines a rock sample and observes: large interlocking crystals of quartz, feldspar, and biotite mica; no visible layering; resistant to chemical weathering. (1) What type of rock (igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic) is this, and what sub-type? (2) Explain the large crystal size in terms of cooling history. (3) Where in the rock cycle did this rock form — at what depth and in what geological setting? (4) Describe TWO processes by which this rock could eventually become a sedimentary rock, and name the sedimentary rock type likely to result. (5) The same rock is subducted to 25 km depth under a convergent margin, experiencing temperatures of 400°C and pressures of ≈8 kbar. Describe what type of rock it would become and the process involved.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) This is granite — an intrusive (plutonic) igneous rock. The combination of quartz, feldspar, and biotite mica is classic felsic igneous composition; the large interlocking crystals are diagnostic of slow cooling.

(2) Large crystals form because the magma cooled very slowly underground — tens of thousands to millions of years for a large pluton to cool. Slow cooling gives crystals time to nucleate and grow large before the magma solidifies. In contrast, basalt (rapidly cooled at the surface) has microscopic crystals; obsidian (instantly quenched) is glassy with no crystals. Crystal size in igneous rocks is a direct proxy for cooling rate.

(3) Granite forms from the cooling of silica-rich (felsic) magma deep in the continental crust — typically 5–40 km depth. Geological settings: continental collision zones (granitic batholiths exposed by erosion of overlying rock over millions of years, e.g. Sierra Nevada batholith), subduction zones (magma derived from partial melting of crust). Never forms at mid-ocean ridges (which produce basaltic magma).

(4) Two pathways to sedimentary rock: (a) Physical weathering and erosion: freeze-thaw, thermal expansion, and abrasion break granite into grains (quartz grains, feldspar fragments). Transported by rivers → deposited → compacted and cemented → sandstone (quartz-rich) or arkose (feldspar-rich sandstone). (b) Chemical weathering: feldspars hydrolyse to clay minerals (kaolinite) in humid climates. Clay minerals transported → deposited in quiet water → compacted → mudstone or shale. Both processes are driven by surface exposure after uplift and erosion of overlying rocks.

(5) At 400°C and 8 kbar, the granite would undergo regional metamorphism — solid-state recrystallisation under heat and pressure without melting. The product would be gneiss — a high-grade metamorphic rock characterised by banding (gneissic foliation) as minerals sort into alternating light (quartz + feldspar) and dark (mica + amphibole) layers under directed pressure. The original granite minerals are destroyed and recrystallised into new metamorphic mineral assemblages stable at these P-T conditions. Gneiss from metamorphosed granite is specifically called orthogneiss.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: The 2011 Tōhoku earthquake (Japan) had a moment magnitude of 9.0 and generated a devastating tsunami. It occurred at the convergent boundary where the Pacific Plate subducts under the North American Plate (the Japan Trench). (1) Explain why subduction zone earthquakes are typically the largest earthquakes on Earth, using the concept of elastic strain accumulation. (2) The Pacific Plate is oceanic; the North American Plate here has continental components. Why does the oceanic plate subduct rather than the continental? (3) Explain the mechanism by which this earthquake generated a tsunami — what happened to the seafloor, and how did this create the wave. (4) Japan has a sophisticated early-warning system that detected the earthquake before the full shaking reached inland cities. This system uses the speed difference between P-waves and S-waves. Explain how this works, and calculate how much warning time residents 150 km from the epicentre would have if P-waves travel at 6 km/s and S-waves at 3.5 km/s. (5) Japan also has extensive subduction-related volcanoes (e.g. Mt Fuji). Explain why subduction generates explosive volcanic eruptions rather than the effusive eruptions at mid-ocean ridges.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) Subduction zones generate the largest earthquakes because the fault area (the subduction interface, or megathrust) is enormous — often hundreds of kilometres long and 100–200 km downdip. The two plates are locked together by friction; as the subducting plate drags down, elastic strain accumulates in the overriding plate (which is compressed and deformed). When friction is overcome and the plates slip, the entire locked fault area ruptures simultaneously. Energy release scales with fault area and slip distance — a megathrust rupturing 500 km length × 150 km width with 20 m average slip releases ≈10²² Joules (Mw 9.0). No other geological process couples such large fault areas over such long strain-accumulation periods (decades to centuries between great earthquakes at a single trench segment).

(2) Oceanic crust is denser (≈3.0 g/cm³, composed of basalt and gabbro) than continental crust (≈2.7 g/cm³, granite-rich). At a convergent boundary, the denser plate sinks into the mantle (negative buoyancy). Additionally, oceanic lithosphere is older and cooler at subduction zones (having moved thousands of km from the mid-ocean ridge) — colder = denser. Continental crust is too buoyant to subduct — when continent meets continent, collision builds mountain ranges instead (Himalayas). The Tōhoku setting is ocean-continent convergence: Pacific (oceanic, dense, old) subducts under North American (partially continental, buoyant).

(3) Tsunami generation: the megathrust fault is nearly horizontal. During the earthquake, the locked segment (100s of km) suddenly slips — the overriding plate, which had been bent downward by elastic strain, snaps upward and seaward, displacing the entire water column above it vertically by several metres over a vast area. This vertical displacement creates the tsunami — a very long-wavelength (100–500 km), low-amplitude (≈1 m in deep ocean) wave that travels at ≈√(gd) ≈ 700 km/h in deep water (d = ocean depth). As the wave approaches shallow water, it slows (conservation of energy → amplitude increases dramatically) → devastating inundation. The 2011 tsunami reached run-up heights of 15–40 m in some coastal areas.

(4) P-waves travel at 6 km/s; S-waves at 3.5 km/s. Time for P-waves to reach 150 km: t_P = 150/6 = 25 seconds. Time for S-waves: t_S = 150/3.5 = 42.9 seconds. Warning time = t_S − t_P = 42.9 − 25 ≈ 18 seconds. The early-warning system detects the first-arriving P-wave, calculates earthquake location and magnitude, and issues alerts before the more destructive S-waves and surface waves arrive. Eighteen seconds is enough to take protective actions (drop-cover-hold, stop trains, trigger automated shutoffs in factories). Tokyo, 400 km away, had ≈1 minute of warning.

(5) Explosivity depends on magma viscosity and volatile (water) content. At mid-ocean ridges: magma is basaltic (low SiO₂, low viscosity, low water content) → gases escape easily → effusive lava flows, gentle eruptions. At subduction zones: the subducting slab carries water-rich sediments and hydrated oceanic crust; as it descends, water is released at depth and lowers the melting point of the overlying mantle wedge → partial melting. But this melt rises through continental crust, picking up silica (felsic contamination) → magma becomes andesitic to rhyolitic (high SiO₂ = high viscosity). High-viscosity magma traps water and CO₂ dissolved as gases under pressure; as magma ascends and pressure drops, gases cannot escape smoothly — explosive decompression → pyroclastic flows, tephra columns. Mt Fuji (andesitic-basaltic) is relatively quiet; more silicic volcanoes (e.g. Mt Pinatubo, Krakatoa) produce catastrophic explosive eruptions.
learningObjectives: Describe Earth's internal structure and explain how seismic waves reveal the properties of each layer.
Explain the three types of plate boundary, the geological features associated with each, and the forces driving plate motion.
Distinguish igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks, and trace rock transformations through the rock cycle.
Explain how tsunami are generated at subduction zones and how P-wave/S-wave speed differences enable earthquake early warning.
commonMistakes: Thinking continents float on liquid rock — the mantle is solid rock that flows ductilely over geological timescales; it behaves as a liquid on million-year timescales but is not molten (except for the outer core and magma chambers).

Confusing magnitude and intensity — magnitude (Richter, Mw) is a measure of energy released at the source; intensity (Mercalli) is the observed shaking at a location, which decreases with distance from the epicentre.
Believing all volcanoes occur at plate boundaries — hotspot volcanoes (Hawaii, Yellowstone) form above mantle plumes far from boundaries; Hawaii is in the middle of the Pacific Plate.

Assuming all earthquakes are caused by tectonic plate motion — intraplate earthquakes (e.g. New Madrid, USA) occur within plates due to ancient fault zones reactivated by residual stress, and can be very large despite being far from any active boundary.
assessmentCriteria: Accurately identifies three plate boundary types with examples and explains the geological features (mountains, trenches, ridges, volcanoes) produced at each.
Correctly classifies rocks, explains the processes forming each type, and traces at least two pathways through the rock cycle.
Explains subduction zone earthquake and tsunami generation mechanistically, linking elastic strain accumulation to sudden release.
Describes how seismic wave types (P, S, surface) differ and how the S-wave shadow zone reveals the liquid outer core.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The gravitational equilibrium between Earth's crust and mantle — like icebergs floating in water, the crust 'floats' on the denser mantle. Thicker continental crust has deeper roots; mountain ranges float high because they have deep crustal keels. When ice sheets melt (removing weight), the crust rises — post-glacial rebound. Scandinavia is still rising ≈1 cm/year following the melting of the last glacial ice sheet 10,000 years ago.

rabbitHoleTerms.term: Subduction Zone Geochemistry and Arc Magmas
rabbitHoleTerms.description: Water released from the subducting slab lowers the melting point of the mantle wedge above (flux melting). The resulting melt is enriched in incompatible elements (K, Na, Ba, Pb) relative to mid-ocean ridge basalts. As the melt rises through the crust, assimilation of continental material increases SiO₂ content. The resulting arc magmas — andesite to dacite to rhyolite — are found in circum-Pacific arcs ('Ring of Fire') and are enriched in the siderophile elements that form metallic ore deposits.

When magma cools, iron-bearing minerals align with Earth's magnetic field, recording the field direction at the time of crystallisation. Seafloor spreading creates symmetric magnetic anomaly stripes about mid-ocean ridges — recording reversals of Earth's magnetic field over geological time. This was the key evidence confirming seafloor spreading and plate tectonics in the 1960s. The geomagnetic reversal record also provides a chronological tool (magnetostratigraphy) for dating sedimentary and igneous sequences.

Over ≈500-million-year cycles, continents assemble into supercontinents (Pangaea, Gondwana, Rodinia, Columbia) and then fragment. Assembly creates mountain ranges at collision zones; fragmentation opens new ocean basins. The supercontinent cycle influences global climate (continental configuration affects ocean and atmosphere circulation), evolution (geographic isolation drives speciation), and the distribution of ore deposits. Pangaea fragmented ≈180 Ma ago; the current arrangement of continents is ≈50–60 million years old.

At mid-ocean ridges, cold seawater infiltrates the oceanic crust, is heated by magma, and re-emerges as superheated (>400°C) vent fluid enriched in dissolved metals and sulfides. Rapid precipitation of sulfides on contact with cold seawater forms black smokers. Chemolithotrophic bacteria oxidise H₂S for energy (not sunlight), forming the base of a unique deep-sea ecosystem — the first known ecosystem independent of solar energy. Hydrothermal vents are also major sites of seafloor mineral deposition (Cu, Zn, Fe, Au).

questions.questionHtml: A geologist finds a rock with fine-grained texture, dark colour, and abundant vesicles (holes left by gas bubbles). What rock type is this, and what does each characteristic tell you about its formation?
options: Granite — formed by slow cooling of felsic magma deep underground; vesicles indicate gas exsolution
Basalt — extrusive igneous rock formed by rapid cooling of mafic lava at Earth's surface; fine grains indicate rapid cooling; vesicles formed as gas escaped before solidification
Shale — sedimentary rock formed from compacted clay; fine grain and vesicles indicate marine origin
Schist — metamorphic rock formed at high pressure; vesicles represent fluid inclusions
questions.correctAnswer: Basalt — extrusive igneous rock formed by rapid cooling of mafic lava at Earth's surface; fine grains indicate rapid cooling; vesicles formed as gas escaped before solidification
questions.explanationHtml: Basalt characteristics: (1) Dark colour — mafic composition (high Mg, Fe; low Si) means abundant dark minerals (pyroxene, olivine, magnetite). (2) Fine-grained texture — rapid cooling at the surface prevents large crystal growth; some basalts have glassy groundmass. (3) Vesicles — dissolved gases (CO₂, H₂O, SO₂) in the lava come out of solution as pressure drops when lava reaches the surface; gas bubbles are trapped as the lava solidifies rapidly. Vesicular basalt is common in lava flows. The presence of vesicles specifically indicates surface/shallow extrusive origin — at depth, pressure prevents gas exsolution. Scoria and pumice are highly vesicular volcanic rocks. Granite is coarse-grained felsic intrusive; shale is sedimentary; schist is metamorphic — none would have these specific features.

questions.questionHtml: The Himalayan mountain range formed when the Indian subcontinent collided with Eurasia ≈50 million years ago. Both plates are continental. Which geological features are characteristic of this type of collision, and why are there no volcanoes in the Himalayas?
options: Volcanoes and deep trenches — continental collision always produces these features regardless of subduction

Very high mountain ranges, deep crustal roots, metamorphic and sedimentary rocks uplifted from sea floor — but no volcanoes, because neither continental plate is dense enough to subduct deeply and generate the water-fluxed melting that produces arc magmas
Moderate mountain ranges and effusive basaltic volcanism — both features of continental collision
Transform faults and strike-slip earthquakes — the Himalayas are a transform boundary, not a convergent one
questions.correctAnswer: Very high mountain ranges, deep crustal roots, metamorphic and sedimentary rocks uplifted from sea floor — but no volcanoes, because neither continental plate is dense enough to subduct deeply and generate the water-fluxed melting that produces arc magmas
questions.explanationHtml: Continent-continent collision: both plates are buoyant felsic crust (density ≈2.7 g/cm³); neither subducts into the denser mantle (≈3.3 g/cm³). Instead, crust thickens — the collision zone crumples like a car crash, piling up to form very high mountains (Everest, K2) with deep crustal roots extending into the mantle (isostasy). Rocks include: metamorphic rocks formed as crust was buried and heated; sedimentary rocks (originally marine sediments from the Tethys Ocean floor) now found at extreme altitude — limestone with marine fossils at 8,000 m elevation. No subduction means no water-rich slab to cause flux melting of the mantle wedge → no arc volcanoes. Compare with the Andes (ocean-continent convergence): Pacific Plate subducts deeply, releases water, generates magma → active volcanic arc. The Tibetan Plateau (world's highest and largest) formed by crustal thickening of the Indian plate underthrusting Eurasia — crust there is ≈70 km thick (vs ≈35 km normal continental crust).

questions.questionHtml: A geologist proposes that an observed sequence of rock layers (oldest at bottom: sandstone → limestone → black shale → coal seam) records a sequence of ancient environments. Reconstruct the environmental history this sequence implies, from oldest to youngest.
options: Deep ocean → shallow tropical sea → swamp/delta → desert (oldest to youngest — the sequence indicates environmental change from marine to continental)
Desert dunes → shallow marine → deep ocean → terrestrial swamp (the grain-size sequence indicates deepening water then shoaling)

Shallow marine/beach → warm shallow sea → restricted/anoxic basin → forested swamp or delta (oldest to youngest — sandstone = high-energy coastal, limestone = warm shallow clear water, black shale = low-oxygen deep/restricted, coal = compressed plant matter from swamp)
Volcanic activity → marine transgression → river delta → glacial lake (consistent with igneous, marine, deltaic, and glacial sedimentary environments)
questions.correctAnswer: Shallow marine/beach → warm shallow sea → restricted/anoxic basin → forested swamp or delta (oldest to youngest — sandstone = high-energy coastal, limestone = warm shallow clear water, black shale = low-oxygen deep/restricted, coal = compressed plant matter from swamp)
questions.explanationHtml: Reading the sedimentary record: (1) Sandstone at base: coarse clastic sediment deposited in a high-energy shallow marine or beach environment — wave and current action sorted and rounded sand grains. (2) Limestone: carbonate rock — precipitated from warm, clear, shallow marine water rich in calcium carbonate, often biogenic (coral reefs, shell material). Transition from sandstone to limestone suggests deeper or clearer water and reduced terrigenous input. (3) Black shale: fine-grained dark sediment rich in organic matter. Dark colour and organic richness indicate deposition in low-oxygen (anoxic) conditions — organic matter preserved rather than oxidised. Could be a stagnant restricted basin, deep water below the oxygen minimum zone, or anoxic sea floor. (4) Coal seam: compressed and diagenetically transformed plant material — formed in a swampy, forested environment (peat → lignite → coal). Indicates the region shallowed to above sea level and became vegetated (classic Carboniferous coal-swamp environment). This sequence records marine transgression (sea advancing over land) followed by regression (sea retreating, terrestrial conditions returning) — a classic sedimentary cycle seen in many coal-bearing basins globally.
